activities.caption: pair each foot with its beat pattern and example
activities.name: poemFeetMatch

config.prompt: The four workhorse feet — pair each with its pulse and its example:

pairs.right: da-da-DUM — two weak beats charging into one strong
DUM-da-da — "SIL-ly po-ems", one strong beat falling away

config.why: Two steps — name the foot, then count: five iambs make iambic pentameter.

activities.anchor: Heaney's "Follower" is a good practice ground
activities.caption: place the line's foot count on the scale
activities.name: poemCountPlace

config.prompt: "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" scans as five clean iambs. Place its foot count:
config.why: Pentameter — the prefix counts feet, not syllables: five iambs make ten syllables. Tetrameter is four feet, trimeter three, hexameter six.

activities.caption: bet on what the missing beat enacts
activities.name: poemBreakPredict

config.q: An otherwise regular line goes quiet for exactly one beat mid-sentence — a missing stress. Read as substitution, that gap most likely…
choices: is a printing error to restore
enacts a loss — the meter performing the meaning
enacts overflow spilling past the line
proves the poem is really free verse
config.why: The steady base meter is audible only so deviations register — a missing beat enacts a loss, a headless opening starts mid-argument, a run of extra syllables enacts overflow.

activities.name: poemPulsePlotter

activities.anchor: builds a problem for eight lines
activities.caption: rebuild Sonnet 18's plan, quatrain by quatrain
activities.name: poemSonnetOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the Shakespearean plan as Sonnet 18 runs it:
items: Quatrain 1 — first analogy: summer too mild
Quatrain 2 — second analogy: too hot, "the eye of heaven shines"
Quatrain 3 — the turn: "But thy eternal summer shall not fade"
Couplet — the boast: "So long lives this, and this gives life to thee"
config.why: Three quatrains stack the analogies and the rhymed couplet snaps the argument shut — where the Shakespearean volta usually lands.

activities.caption: drag the divider — two different freedoms
activities.name: poemFreedomCompare

config.prompt: Both are unrhymed — drag the divider to hear the difference:

before.label: Blank verse — unrhymed, strictly metered
before.text: Iambic pentameter, the line of Milton, Wordsworth and Shakespeare's plays: rhyme set aside, the meter keeps dignity and momentum — read a hundred lines of Paradise Lost aloud and the pulse never leaves.

after.label: Free verse — the meter dropped
after.text: Whitman and the moderns choose line by line: patterns of breath, image and line-break. Eliot's quip is a technical claim — no verse is free for the man who wants to do a good job.

config.why: "Unrhymed" and "unmetered" are different freedoms — the difference is audible.

activities.anchor: bind words by sound and so bind meanings
activities.caption: file each effect by the channel it repeats
activities.name: poemSoundBuckets

config.prompt: Three channels of poetic music — file each case:

items.label: Coleridge's "the furrow followed free" — f after f after f
the same vowel ringing down a line of verse
a run of words ending in the same hard consonant
"grim" and "grand" linked by their opening gr-
a wave in the mouth — the ship moving as the sounds move

config.why: When the same consonant links two unlike words, it is quietly asserting a kinship the sense denies.

activities.anchor: two structural decisions modern poetry leans on hardest
activities.caption: true or false — the line-break decisions
activities.name: poemLineJudge

statements.s: The word at an enjambed break belongs to two lines at once.
statements.why: Running the sentence over the break creates momentum and double meaning.

statements.s: An end-stopped line closes like a door.
statements.why: The sense completes at the line's edge instead of spilling over.

statements.s: A caesura is a hard pause at the end of a line.
statements.why: It is a hard pause inside the line, often marked by punctuation — it splits the beat where the mind splits.

statements.s: Comparing two poems on the enjambment axis alone gives you half a comparison.
statements.why: Where a poem's lines break and breathe is as meaningful as where they rhyme.
